topic: Introduction to Fire Insurance and Fire Hazards
t: The 'fire tetrahedron' adds a fourth element to the traditional fire triangle of fuel, heat and oxygen. That fourth element is:
e: Combustion is sustained by a self-propagating chemical chain reaction; extinguishing agents like dry chemical powder work by interrupting this chain reaction rather than by cooling or smothering.

topic: Introduction to Fire Insurance and Fire Hazards
t: Which of the following is the most typical example of a material liable to spontaneous combustion?
o: Steel scrap stored in the open
Cement bags in a dry godown
Oil-soaked cotton rags or a large stockpile of coal
e: Materials such as oily rags, coal heaps, haystacks and oilseed cakes generate heat by slow oxidation or fermentation and can ignite without an external source. This is why spontaneous combustion is excluded from the basic fire peril.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: A lightning strike cracks the chimney of an insured factory without causing any fire. Under the SFSP policy this damage is:
o: Covered, because lightning is a named peril irrespective of whether fire results
Not covered, as no fire occurred
Covered only under the earthquake add-on
Covered only if the chimney was specifically insured
e: Lightning is the second named peril and covers direct damage by lightning whether or not fire ensues. The earthquake add-on is unrelated.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: During a riot, a mob breaks into an insured shop, damages fixtures and carries away stock worth ₹2 lakh. Under the riot, strike and malicious damage peril of the SFSP policy:
o: Both the damage to fixtures and the stolen stock are covered
Damage to fixtures is covered, but loss by burglary, housebreaking, theft or larceny is excluded
Only the stolen stock is covered
Nothing is covered as riot losses require a separate policy
e: The RSMD peril covers physical damage by rioters but specifically excludes loss by burglary, housebreaking, theft or larceny, and loss due to cessation of work.

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: Under the 'aircraft damage' peril of the SFSP policy, which of the following is excluded?
o: Damage by an aircraft crashing on the premises
Damage by articles dropped from an aircraft
Damage caused by pressure waves from aircraft travelling at supersonic speed
e: Aircraft damage covers loss by aircraft, aerial devices and articles dropped from them, but excludes damage caused by pressure waves (sonic boom).

topic: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy – Coverage and Exclusions
t: A fire in a small factory causes an assessed loss of ₹45,000. After applying the standard policy excess for non-AOG perils, the amount payable under the SFSP policy is:
e: For perils other than AOG perils the excess is a flat ₹10,000 for each and every loss, giving ₹45,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹35,000. The 5% basis applies only to AOG perils.

t: Under a Declaration policy on stocks, the provisional premium collected at inception is:
o: 100% of the annual premium on the sum insured
50% of the annual premium on the sum insured
75% of the annual premium on the sum insured, adjustable on expiry
e: A declaration policy is issued on payment of a provisional premium of 75% of the annual premium, which is later adjusted on the basis of the average of monthly declarations.

t: Under the SFSP policy, expenses for removal of debris are automatically covered up to what percentage of the claim amount?
e: Debris removal cost is included up to 1% of the claim amount; expenses above this limit must be insured by a specific add-on with a separate sum insured.

t: Architects', surveyors' and consulting engineers' fees incurred in reinstating damaged property are automatically covered under the SFSP policy up to:
e: Such professional fees are covered up to 3% of the claim amount; fees in excess of 3% can be insured under an add-on cover.

t: A building is insured for ₹3 crore at a fire rate of ₹0.60 per mille. The basic annual premium, before GST, is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). 'Per mille' means per thousand rupees of sum insured: ₹3,00,00,000 ÷ 1,000 × 0.60 = ₹18,000. GST at 18% would be added on top.

t: The add-on cover for 'omission to insure additions, alterations or extensions' automatically covers such additions to buildings and machinery during the policy period up to:
e: This add-on protects the insured who adds assets during the year without informing the insurer, up to 5% of the sum insured on the respective item, with premium adjusted at expiry.

t: Long-term fire policies (for periods exceeding one year, with a discount on premium) are available in respect of:
o: Any risk with sum insured above ₹1 crore
e: Long-term policies with scaled discounts are permitted only for dwellings; commercial and industrial risks are insured on annual policies.

topic: Standard Products – Bharat Griha Raksha, Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha
t: Under Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha, underinsurance is waived if the sum insured is not less than what percentage of the value of the insured property?
e: The product waives underinsurance up to 15%, so no proportionate reduction is made if the sum insured is at least 85% of the value at risk. Beyond this, average applies.

topic: Standard Products – Bharat Griha Raksha, Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha
t: Under Bharat Griha Raksha, general home contents are automatically covered without any declaration for:
o: 10% of the building sum insured, subject to a maximum of ₹5 lakh
20% of the building sum insured, subject to a maximum of ₹10 lakh
50% of the building sum insured without any limit
e: The product includes general contents at 20% of the home building sum insured up to ₹10 lakh automatically; a higher amount or valuable contents must be declared and insured separately.

t: The SFSP policy provides that in case of misdescription, misrepresentation or non-disclosure of any material particular, the policy shall be:
o: Automatically cancelled with refund of premium
Continued but with the sum insured reduced
Voidable at the option of the insurer
Valid but the claim reduced by 25%
e: Condition 1 makes the policy voidable in case of misdescription or non-disclosure of material facts, reflecting the principle of utmost good faith.

t: If an insured building or part of it falls or is displaced (other than by an insured peril), the insurance on that building ceases unless the insured notifies the insurer and the insurer agrees to continue, within:
e: The 'fall or displacement' condition gives the insured 7 days to notify the event and obtain the insurer's agreement to continue cover; otherwise the insurance on the building ceases.

t: An insured cancels an annual SFSP policy after 3 months. The refund of premium will be calculated:
o: By retaining premium at the short period scale for the time on risk
On a pro-rata basis for the unexpired period
No refund is allowed on cancellation by the insured
e: When the insured cancels, the insurer retains premium at short period rates (40% for 3 months) and refunds the balance; pro-rata refund applies only when the insurer cancels.

t: A fire claim is rejected by the insurer in writing. Under the policy conditions, the insured's right to recover is forfeited unless the claim is made the subject of a suit or arbitration within:
o: 12 months of the date of loss
e: The fire policy contains a 12-month limitation condition running from the date of rejection, after which the claim is deemed abandoned and the insurer's liability ends.

t: After settling a fire claim caused by the negligence of a contractor, the insurer sues the contractor in the insured's name to recover the amount paid. This right flows from the policy condition on:
e: Subrogation entitles the insurer, after indemnifying the insured, to step into the insured's shoes and pursue recovery from a third party responsible for the loss.

t: A building insured for ₹60 lakh under an SFSP policy is found at the time of fire to be worth ₹80 lakh. The assessed loss is ₹16 lakh. Ignoring excess, the amount payable under the condition of average is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Under average the claim is reduced in the ratio of sum insured to value: ₹16 lakh × 60/80 = ₹12 lakh. The insured bears the remaining ₹4 lakh as his own insurer.

t: A shop is insured for ₹50 lakh at a rate of ₹1.20 per mille. The total premium payable including GST at 18% is:
Under the All India Fire Tariff, the primary factor determining the basic rate for an industrial or manufacturing risk is:
o: The occupancy, i.e. the nature of the process or trade carried on
e: Tariff rates are occupancy-based, with loadings for hazardous construction and storage and discounts for fire protection. Sum insured affects the premium amount but not the rate.

t: A fire policy is required for a period of 2 months. Under the short period scale, the premium charged is what percentage of the annual premium?
e: The short period scale charges 30% of the annual premium for a period of up to 2 months; 15% applies to 1 month and 40% to 3 months.

t: A manufacturing unit has stopped all production for an extended period but still wishes to insure its building and machinery. In fire tariff terminology such a risk is rated as a:
e: Factories in which no manufacturing activity is carried on continuously for 30 days or more are treated as silent risks and rated at a special lower rate, since process hazards are absent.

t: Which of the following persons does NOT have insurable interest in a building for the purpose of fire insurance?
o: A mortgagee who has lent money against the building
A lessee who is liable for repairs under the lease
A trustee holding the building for beneficiaries
An unsecured trade creditor of the owner
e: An unsecured creditor has no legal or equitable interest in the specific property and would not suffer loss by its destruction, so he cannot insure it. Mortgagees, lessees and trustees all have insurable interest.

t: A warehouse keeper insures goods belonging to various customers lying in his warehouse. His insurable interest arises in the capacity of:
e: A bailee in lawful possession of goods is responsible for them and may insure them for their full value, holding any excess over his own interest for the owners.

t: A document attached to a fire policy to record a change in the sum insured, location or other terms after issue of the policy is known as:
e: Endorsements modify or add to the terms of an existing policy; they are used for mid-term changes such as increase in sum insured, change of address or addition of perils.

topic: Consequential Loss Insurance – Principles and Concepts
t: A company's annual gross profit is ₹24 lakh and it selects an indemnity period of 18 months. The sum insured under its consequential loss policy should be:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). When the indemnity period exceeds 12 months, the sum insured must be the annual gross profit increased proportionately: ₹24 lakh × 18/12 = ₹36 lakh.

t: A proposer for fire insurance does not mention that the premises had suffered two fires in the previous three years. The insurer's remedy is based on breach of the principle of:
e: Previous loss history is a material fact that must be disclosed under utmost good faith; non-disclosure makes the policy voidable at the insurer's option.

t: Water used by the fire brigade to extinguish a fire in the insured premises damages stock that was not touched by the fire. Under the SFSP policy this water damage is:
o: Not covered, since the policy does not cover water damage
Covered only under the bursting of water tanks peril
Covered only if a separate water damage add-on is taken
Covered, because fire is the proximate cause of the damage
e: Damage caused by reasonable measures to extinguish or prevent spread of fire, including water damage and property damaged by fire-fighters, is attributable to the fire as proximate cause.

t: When an insurer pays a claim on the basis of total loss of goods, the salvage of the damaged goods:
o: Belongs to the insurer, which may dispose of it and retain the proceeds
Belongs to the insured, who may sell it and keep the proceeds
Must be destroyed under supervision of the surveyor
Belongs jointly to insurer and insured in equal shares
e: Having paid for the goods in full, the insurer is entitled to the salvage; alternatively the salvage value is deducted from the claim and the goods left with the insured.

t: Stock insured for ₹40 lakh under an SFSP policy is valued at ₹50 lakh at the time of a fire, which causes a loss of ₹5 lakh. After applying average and the policy excess, the amount payable is:
e: Average reduces the claim to ₹5 lakh × 40/50 = ₹4,00,000; the flat excess of ₹10,000 for the fire peril is then deducted, leaving ₹3,90,000.

t: Under the reinstatement value clause, the insured must commence and carry out reinstatement with reasonable despatch and complete it within what period from the date of destruction, unless extended by the insurer?
e: Reinstatement must be completed within 12 months (or such further time as the insurer allows); until the cost is actually incurred, the insurer's liability remains on the indemnity (market value) basis.

topic: Consequential Loss Insurance – Principles and Concepts
t: Which of the following is a standing charge that would normally be insured under a consequential loss policy?
e: Standing charges are fixed expenses such as rent, rates, salaries, interest and depreciation that continue even when turnover falls. Purchases, carriage and packing vary with turnover and are uninsured working expenses.

topic: Consequential Loss Insurance – Principles and Concepts
t: 'Standard turnover' under a consequential loss policy means the turnover during:
o: The twelve months immediately before the date of damage
The period in the twelve months immediately before the damage that corresponds with the indemnity period
The financial year immediately before the damage
e: Standard turnover is the base against which actual turnover during the indemnity period is compared to compute shortage; annual turnover (12 months before damage) is used for the underinsurance test.

topic: Consequential Loss Insurance – Principles and Concepts
t: For applying the underinsurance (average) provision in a CL policy with a 12-month indemnity period, the sum insured is compared with gross profit on the 'annual turnover', which is the turnover during:
o: The twelve months immediately before the date of the damage
The twelve months after the date of the damage
e: Annual turnover is defined as turnover during the 12 months immediately preceding the damage, adjusted for trend; if the indemnity period exceeds 12 months it is increased proportionately.

t: Section 64VB of the Insurance Act 1938 requires that:
o: Premium is received in advance before the risk is assumed
Every policy carries a free-look clause
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). No risk may be assumed unless the premium has been received in advance or is guaranteed in the manner prescribed.

topic: Consequential Loss Insurance – Principles and Concepts
t: Under a consequential loss policy, 'turnover' is defined as:
o: Net sales after deducting all discounts and taxes
Total receipts including sale of fixed assets
Money paid or payable to the insured for goods sold and delivered and services rendered in the course of the business at the premises
e: Turnover is the trading revenue of the business carried on at the insured premises; capital receipts such as sale of fixed assets are excluded.

topic: Consequential Loss Policy – Coverage, Specification and Extensions
t: A fire in a neighbouring godown causes the municipal authorities to cordon off the street, and customers cannot reach the insured's showroom for three weeks though the showroom itself is undamaged. This loss can be covered under the CL policy extension for:
e: The prevention of access extension covers interruption caused by insured damage to property in the vicinity of the premises that hinders access to them, even though the insured's own property is undamaged.

topic: Consequential Loss Policy – Coverage, Specification and Extensions
t: A factory's production is interrupted because a fire at the State electricity board's substation cuts off power supply for ten days. Cover for such a loss requires the CL policy extension for:
o: Public utilities (failure of electricity, water or gas supply)
e: The public utilities extension covers interruption due to insured damage at the premises of the electricity, water or gas undertaking supplying the insured, usually subject to a time excess.

topic: Consequential Loss Policy – Coverage, Specification and Extensions
t: The specification of a consequential loss policy may include a separate item for 'auditors' fees'. This item covers:
o: Fees for the annual statutory audit of the insured's accounts
Fees of the surveyor appointed by the insurer
Reasonable charges payable by the insured to auditors for producing and certifying particulars required by the insurer for a claim
Fees of the arbitrator in case of dispute
e: Auditors' fees cover the cost of preparing claim information from the insured's books; routine audit fees are a standing charge and the insurer bears its own surveyor's fees.

topic: Consequential Loss Policy – Coverage, Specification and Extensions
t: Under the 'dual basis' of insuring wages in a CL policy, wages are covered:
o: Only for the first four weeks of interruption
On a pro-rata basis with gross profit
At 100% for an initial period and at a reduced percentage for the remainder of the indemnity period, with an option of consolidation
e: The dual basis recognises that the insured may keep the full workforce for a short period and then retain only a percentage of wages; the consolidated period option allows combining the two.

t: After a fire, an insured hires temporary premises at a cost of ₹2,00,000, thereby avoiding a reduction in turnover of ₹5,00,000. The rate of gross profit is 30%. The increased cost of working recoverable under the CL policy is:
e: ICOW is limited to the gross profit that would otherwise have been lost: ₹5,00,000 × 30% = ₹1,50,000. The balance ₹50,000 is uneconomic and not recoverable under the basic item.

t: Nomination and assignment of a life insurance policy are governed respectively by which sections of the Insurance Act 1938?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Section 39 deals with nomination; Section 38 with assignment and transfer.

t: During the indemnity period the insured ceases to pay a factory rent of ₹1,00,000 which had been included in the insured standing charges. In the CL claim this amount is:
o: Added to the claim as increased cost of working
Deducted from the claim as a saving in insured standing charges
Ignored, as it does not affect turnover
Paid separately to the landlord by the insurer
e: The policy indemnifies only actual loss; any insured standing charge that ceases or is reduced in consequence of the damage is deducted from the amount otherwise payable.

t: A business insures gross profit for ₹30 lakh with an indemnity period of 24 months. Gross profit on the adjusted annual turnover is ₹20 lakh. An assessed loss of ₹4 lakh will be paid as:
e: With a 24-month indemnity period the required sum insured is ₹20 lakh × 24/12 = ₹40 lakh. The insured is underinsured, so the claim is reduced to ₹4 lakh × 30/40 = ₹3 lakh.

t: Compared with a conventional consequential loss (fire) policy, the business interruption section of an Industrial All Risks policy additionally covers interruption following:
o: Loss of market after the indemnity period
e: The IAR BI section follows the all-risks material damage section and therefore responds to interruption caused by machinery breakdown as well as fire and special perils.

t: Which of the following is a standard exclusion under the material damage section of the Industrial All Risks policy?
o: Shortages discovered only on stock-taking or inventory
e: IAR is written on an all-risks basis with named exclusions such as inventory shortages, wear and tear, gradual deterioration, faulty design known to the insured and war; flood, burglary and boiler explosion are covered.

t: The most suitable portable extinguisher for a fire in a live electrical switchboard is:
e: CO2 is non-conductive and leaves no residue, making it suitable for electrical fires. Water and foam conduct electricity and risk electrocution; ABC dry powder is also acceptable.

t: Under the Petroleum Act, 1934 and Rules, 'Class A' petroleum is petroleum having a flash point:
e: Class A petroleum (e.g. petrol) has a flash point below 23°C, Class B from 23°C to below 65°C (e.g. kerosene, diesel) and Class C from 65°C to below 93°C; petroleum with flash point of 93°C and above is excluded petroleum.
